steps.explanationAfterStep: Hydroxide adds to the nitrile carbon, as it would to a carbonyl carbon. One C≡N π bond moves onto nitrogen, giving an imidate anion (an aza-enolate of an amide).
Water protonates the strongly basic nitrogen. The product, HO–C=NH, is an imidic acid, the tautomer of a primary amide.
Hydroxide removes the O–H proton. The O⁻ now sits on the carbon next to the C–Cl carbon, ready to attack it from inside the molecule.

An intramolecular SN2: the O⁻ displaces chloride from the neighbouring carbon, exactly as a halohydrin closes to an epoxide. Outside attack on this caged tertiary carbon is impossible; a neighbouring nucleophile held next to it succeeds.

Removing the N–H proton re-forms the C≡N, and the strained ring opens onto oxygen. The oxygen is now on the ring carbon that carried chlorine: the chlorine has been replaced by an oxygen, with the nitrile acting as a carrier.
A cyanohydrin anion falls apart to the ketone and cyanide. The carbon that carried Cl and CN is now a C=O: the 2-chloroacrylonitrile has done the job of ketene.

title: Unmasking the ketone
subtitle: Hydroxide turns the α-chloronitrile of the Diels–Alder adduct into a ketone
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 34 (ketene equivalents in Diels–Alder reactions)
E. J. Corey, N. M. Weinshenker, T. K. Schaaf and W. Huber, Stereo-controlled synthesis of dl-prostaglandins F2α and E2, J. Am. Chem. Soc., 1969, 91, 5675–5677

products.caption: bicyclo[2.2.1]hept-5-en-2-one with the CH₂OMe bridge + cyanide + chloride

iminolate.caption: the iminolate: O⁻ next to the carbon carrying the chlorine
hintTiers: This is like epoxide formation from a halohydrin: an O⁻ on one carbon displaces a halide from the next carbon.
The oxygen attacks the carbon carrying the chlorine from the back of the C–Cl bond; chloride leaves. A three-membered ring with oxygen forms.
Oxygen lone pair → new bond to the carbon carrying Cl; the C–Cl bond → lone pair on chlorine.
iminolate.learnerPrompt: The O⁻ and the C–Cl bond are on neighbouring carbons. Close a ring.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: The charge, and the most reactive lone pair, is on oxygen. The oxygen closes the ring.
Hydroxide still cannot reach the back of the C–Cl bond from outside the cage. Inside the molecule, the neighbouring O⁻ can.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right: the oxygen attacks. That carbon now has five bonds: the C–Cl bond must break.

reactants.caption: the α-chloronitrile (Diels–Alder adduct) + KOH in aqueous DMSO
hintTiers: The carbon carrying Cl and CN is tertiary and sits in a cage: nothing can reach the back of its C–Cl bond. Look for an electrophilic carbon that is easy to reach.
A nitrile carbon is electrophilic, like a carbonyl carbon: a nucleophile adds to it and one π bond of the C≡N moves onto nitrogen.
Hydroxide oxygen lone pair → new bond to the nitrile carbon; one C≡N π bond → lone pair on nitrogen.
reactants.learnerPrompt: Hydroxide starts the unmasking. Where does it add?

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: SN2 at this carbon is impossible: it is tertiary, and the bicyclic cage blocks the back of the C–Cl bond. Hydroxide adds to the nitrile carbon instead.
Chloride cannot simply leave: the cation would sit next to an electron-withdrawing nitrile. The chloride leaves later, pushed out by a neighbouring oxygen.
The methyl ether is a remote protecting group and takes no part. The electrophile next to the C–Cl carbon is the nitrile carbon.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right atom. Carbon would now have five bonds: one π bond of the C≡N must move onto nitrogen.

imidic-acid.caption: the imidic acid HO–C=NH + hydroxide
hintTiers: The O–H of an imidic acid is acidic, like a carboxylic acid O–H, and hydroxide is now present.
Hydroxide takes the proton from the oxygen, leaving an O⁻ next to the C–Cl carbon.
Hydroxide lone pair → new bond to the O–H hydrogen; that O–H bond → lone pair on oxygen.
imidic-acid.learnerPrompt: Make the oxygen nucleophilic: remove its proton.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: That only undoes the last step. Take the proton from oxygen instead, to make an alkoxide-like nucleophile.
A neutral OH is a poor nucleophile, and the oxygen would end up positive. Remove its proton first.

iminooxirane.caption: an oxiran-2-imine (a three-membered ring with oxygen) + chloride
hintTiers: Removing the N–H proton gives nitrogen a lone pair it can push towards carbon. The ring C–O bond is strained and can break.
In one step: hydroxide takes the N–H proton, the N–H bond becomes a second C=N π bond (a C≡N again), and the ring C–O bond breaks onto oxygen.
Hydroxide lone pair → new bond to the N–H hydrogen; the N–H bond → π bond C=N; the ring C–O bond to the C=N carbon → lone pair on oxygen.
iminooxirane.learnerPrompt: Hydroxide removes the N–H proton. What happens to the strained ring?

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Hydroxide could add to the C=N, but removing the N–H proton and opening the strained ring is faster and leads straight on.
Breaking that C–O bond would leave a cation next to a C=N. Use the nitrogen: once its proton is gone it can push electrons into the ring carbon.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Good: the nitrile is re-forming. Its carbon now has five bonds: break the ring C–O bond onto oxygen.

imidate-anion.caption: the imidate anion: the negative charge sits on nitrogen
hintTiers: An N⁻ is a much stronger base than hydroxide, and the solvent contains water.
Water gives a proton to the nitrogen and becomes hydroxide.
Nitrogen lone pair → new bond to a hydrogen of water; that O–H bond → lone pair on the water oxygen.
imidate-anion.learnerPrompt: The negative nitrogen is a strong base. Protonate it.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Taking the O–H proton now would make a dianion. First let the negative nitrogen take a proton from water.
A proton does not hop between two atoms of one O–C=N unit: the geometry is poor. Protons move through the water around the molecule.

cyanohydrin-anion.caption: the deprotonated cyanohydrin of the ketone
hintTiers: A cyanohydrin is a ketone that has added HCN. In base the reverse is fast: the alkoxide pushes cyanide out.
The O⁻ lone pair makes a C=O π bond; the bond to the nitrile carbon breaks and cyanide leaves.
Oxygen lone pair → C=O π bond; the C–CN bond → lone pair on the nitrile carbon (cyanide).
cyanohydrin-anion.learnerPrompt: The alkoxide is next to a C–CN bond. Finish the unmasking.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: A ring CH₂ cannot leave as a carbanion. Cyanide is the group that leaves: its negative charge sits on an sp carbon next to nitrogen.
A bridgehead carbon cannot leave as a carbanion. Cyanide leaves, a stable anion.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right: the C=O forms. Now one bond from that carbon must break: which group is the best leaving group?

mechanismSummary: Corey heated the Diels–Alder adduct with potassium hydroxide in aqueous DMSO to reveal bicyclo[2.2.1]hept-5-en-2-one. The route drawn here is a reasonable polar mechanism for this unmasking; the problem set's card says why the detailed route is a model. Hydroxide adds to the nitrile; proton transfers give an iminolate O⁻; that oxygen displaces chloride from the neighbouring carbon, closing a three-membered ring, the only way to substitute this caged tertiary carbon; removing the N–H proton opens the ring again to the cyanohydrin anion, which loses cyanide to give the ketone. Overall the carbon that carried Cl and CN becomes a C=O, so 2-chloroacrylonitrile served as a ketene equivalent. The ring-closing SN2 inverts the carbon it attacks, but the epimers of the adduct all give the same ketone (not checked by the app yet).
